hero.highlight.text: doesn't always get the same answer.

hero.takeaway.text: The model's answer is drawn one token at a time. A single run is just one sample, so repeat it before drawing a conclusion.

concepts.01-sample.description.text: Sampling: for every token it writes, the model draws one from the probability distribution over candidate tokens. If this step draws something different, everything written after it changes too.

concepts.02-temperature.description.text: Temperature decides how the draw is made: the lower it is, the more it favors the highest-probability candidate; the higher it is, the more spread out the draw. It changes nothing in the request.

concepts.03-zero.description.text: With temperature at 0 the answer is usually very stable, but the provider does not guarantee it is identical character for character every time.

concepts.04-repeat.description.text: A controlled experiment changes only one condition. But the answer itself fluctuates, so run each arm several times before comparing.

section-1.title.text: The same request can get different answers

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: Send the same request again, unchanged, and the answer may differ. When {{lesson:chat-request}} compared "With system prompt" and "Remove the system prompt", each arm was run only once. The two answers had different lengths, but was that caused by the system prompt, or would the same request vary like that anyway? Those two runs alone can't tell you.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: This lesson takes that question on its own. It calls no tools and does just one thing: send the same request unchanged 5 times and count how many different answers come back. The request body is built only once, the messages in all 5 sends are identical character for character, and the previous answer is never carried into the next one. If the answers still differ, the difference can only come from the provider's side, not from the request.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: This matters a lot for the later lessons. Every step of an agent is decided by a model request: what to do next, which tool to use, when to finish. If the answer at any one step changes, the following steps go down a different path. When the same task succeeds this time and fails next time, the cause is often not broken code but the model giving a different answer at some step.

section-2.title.text: The answer is drawn one token at a time

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: The model writes its answer one token at a time, and each token is a draw. Here is a made-up example: naming a cat-supplies shop, the model must first write the first token. To keep the arithmetic easy, suppose there are only four candidate tokens, and the model gives them probabilities of 44% for "Meow", 32% for "Cat", 16% for "Cute", and 8% for "Pet". Then it draws one according to those probabilities: out of 100 draws, about 44 give "Meow" and about 8 give "Pet".

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: The token drawn is attached to the end of what has been written, the model computes the probabilities for the next step, draws again, and continues until it writes a token that means the end or fills the length limit. The finish_reason you saw in {{lesson:chat-request}} records how this last step stopped. Even a two-word shop name takes several draws in a row.

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: The key point is that every step depends on what has already been written. If the first token drawn is "Meow", the model is more likely to write "Mart" or "Star" next; if it's "Cat", what follows continues from "Cat". A difference of one token at step one sends the whole name down a different path. The longer the answer, the more draws there are, and the more chances two runs have to differ.

section-2.paragraphs.3.text: The probability here is the model's estimate of "what to write as the next token". It is not the probability that "this answer is correct". The highest-probability candidate is not necessarily the best, and a low-probability one is not necessarily wrong. This lesson only observes how the way of drawing causes differences. It doesn't judge which shop name is better.

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: Whether you want a stable answer or a look at several phrasings is set by temperature in the request: it is the sampling temperature, and it decides how concentrated the probability-based draw is. Different tasks want different things. When pulling a date out of a piece of text or deciding which tool to use, you want the same answer every time. When naming a shop or thinking of a title, you actually want to see several different phrasings.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: Temperature sharpens or flattens the probability distribution, but it doesn't change the ranking. Using the made-up example from the previous section: temperature 1 is the original set of probabilities. Lower the temperature to 0.5 and "Meow" rises to about 58% while "Pet" falls below 2%. Raise it to 1.3 and "Meow" falls to about 40% while "Pet" rises to about 11%. At temperature 0, implementations usually just take the highest-probability candidate at each step. How these numbers are computed is in the deep dive below.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: This lesson's runner writes temperature into the request body along with messages. One exercise sets it to 0 and the other to 1.3. Inputs limits the range to 0 through 2, and a value outside the range is rejected before the request is sent. The allowed range and default differ somewhat between providers, so go by each one's documentation.

section-3.paragraphs.3.text: Temperature changes only the draw, not the information in the request. The messages sent in both arms are exactly the same, and the model knows just as much. A high temperature makes answers more varied, which does not make the model smarter. At very high temperatures, candidates with very low probability that don't fit are also more likely to be drawn, so strict tasks generally use a low temperature. This lesson only counts how many answers there are. It doesn't judge quality.

deep-dive-softmax.title.text: By hand: how scores become probabilities, and what temperature changes

deep-dive-softmax.summary.text: Work through the scores of four candidate tokens: first convert them to probabilities, then see how temperature changes them.

deep-dive-softmax.paragraphs.0.text: At each step the model first gives every candidate token a score. Scores can be positive or negative and don't add up to 1, so they have to be converted to probabilities. The usual method is called Softmax: for each score, raise the constant e (about 2.718) to that score, then divide by the sum of all the results. Exponentiation makes every result positive, and a small difference in score becomes a big difference in the result.

deep-dive-softmax.paragraphs.1.text: A made-up example. The scores of four candidates are: "Meow" 2.0, "Cat" 1.7, "Cute" 1.0, "Pet" 0.3. After exponentiation they are about 7.39, 5.47, 2.72, and 1.35, which sum to 16.93. Dividing each one gives 44%, 32%, 16%, and 8%, the set of probabilities used in the text.

deep-dive-softmax.paragraphs.2.text: Temperature acts before the exponentiation: first divide every score by the temperature. At temperature 0.5 the scores become 4.0, 3.4, 2.0, and 0.6, the gaps doubled, and the results come out to about 58%, 32%, 8%, and 2%. At temperature 1.3 the scores become about 1.54, 1.31, 0.77, and 0.23, the gaps shrink, and the results are about 40%, 31%, 18%, and 11%. Temperature 1 leaves everything as is.

deep-dive-softmax.paragraphs.3.text: The closer the temperature is to 0, the more the top score's lead is magnified: at temperature 0.2, "Meow" already takes about 81% and "Cute" and "Pet" together are under 1%. At exactly temperature 0 you can't divide, so implementations usually switch to taking the highest-scoring candidate at each step. The order of the four candidates never changed: temperature changes the gaps, not the ranking.

deep-dive-softmax.paragraphs.4.text: This also explains why the shop names in the high-temperature arm vary more. A shop name takes several tokens, and a high temperature gives the lower-ranked candidates a bigger share at every step, so every step is more likely to go astray. The detours stack up, and you get more different answers.

predict-request-count.prompt.text: Run it once first. In the experiment "Low and high temperature, 5 runs each", before you run "temperature set to 0", guess: how many model requests (request events) will this run send?

mq-what-temperature-changes.what-tempera.text: The two arms' requests differ only in temperature. The 5 answers in the high-temperature arm vary more. What does that show?
A high temperature spreads the draw out, so the differences in the answers come from sampling
Correct. The request content is the same, so the difference can only come from how the draw is made.
The high-temperature arm's request gave the model more information
Not quite. The messages in the two arms are exactly the same, and temperature adds no information.
The high-temperature arm used a smarter model
Not quite. Both arms use the same model; only the way of drawing is different.
Temperature adjusts the sampling method. The information in the request does not change at all.

deep-dive-top-p.summary.text: Two other common parameters for the draw: first cut off the lower-ranked candidates, then draw from what remains.

deep-dive-top-p.paragraphs.0.text: Temperature doesn't reduce the candidates. It only changes each one's share, and however high the temperature, the last-ranked candidate still has a chance of being drawn. Two other methods cut the tail off directly. Top-k keeps only the few highest-probability candidates; for example, top_k=2 keeps just the first two. Top-p sorts the candidates by probability from high to low and adds them up one at a time, stopping once the sum reaches the given threshold; for example, top_p=0.9 stops when it reaches 90%. After the cut, the probabilities of the remaining candidates are scaled up proportionally to total 100%, and the draw is made from them.

deep-dive-top-p.paragraphs.1.text: With the made-up example from the text, the original probabilities are 44%, 32%, 16%, and 8%. top_k=2 leaves only "Meow" and "Cat", which after redistribution are about 58% and 42%. top_p=0.9 accumulates 44%, 76%, then 92%, stopping at "Cute", so "Pet" is cut and the remaining three are about 48%, 35%, and 17%.

deep-dive-top-p.paragraphs.2.text: The two differ in what they do when the shape of the distribution changes. Top-k always keeps the same number; if at some step "Meow" alone takes 95%, the other candidates it keeps are all very marginal. Top-p follows the shape: when the distribution is sharp it keeps only one or two, and when it is flat it keeps more.

deep-dive-top-p.paragraphs.3.text: In a request, OpenAI-compatible APIs usually have a top_p field, and some providers also accept top_k. The request in this lesson sets only temperature and uses the provider's defaults for everything else. Some providers' documentation suggests adjusting only one of temperature and top_p at a time, because otherwise you can't tell which one had the effect. It is the same reasoning as a controlled experiment changing only one condition.

section-4.title.text: Temperature 0 doesn't guarantee the same answer

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: With temperature set to 0, answers are usually very stable, but the provider does not guarantee they are identical character for character every time. Many people set temperature to 0 because they want the same request to get the same answer every time, for testing and comparing. At that point the variation no longer comes from the draw but from the step that computes the probabilities.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: At temperature 0 each step takes the highest-probability candidate. If two candidates have nearly tied scores, a tiny error in the last few decimal places of the computation can flip their order. That kind of error really exists: the provider's servers do massive parallel computation and also batch together requests that arrive at the same time. Which requests yours is batched with and in what order the additions are done can differ each time. Once one step picks a different candidate, everything after it differs.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: Reasoning models add another layer. The reasoning is also drawn one token at a time, so even when the final shop name is the same, how much reasoning is written can differ a lot from run to run. The last column of the lab report's table is the completion tokens of each run, and the tokens used for reasoning are counted in it. Also, some providers don't allow changing the temperature for this kind of model and return an error if you pass it; others accept it but it has no effect.

section-4.paragraphs.3.text: "The 5 answers at temperature 0 were all the same" is only an observation about this one run. A different-answer count of 1 in the lab report says these 5 were the same. It doesn't say the 6th will be too, and if the provider updates the model under the same name the result may change as well. To use the model's answers in a test, check conditions the program can verify, such as whether the format is right, instead of requiring them to be identical character for character.

deep-dive-zero.title.text: Why temperature 0 can still be inconsistent

deep-dive-zero.summary.text: Add decimals in a different order on a computer and the result can differ slightly. A slight difference can switch to a different candidate.

deep-dive-zero.paragraphs.0.text: Try it in Python: (0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3 gives 0.6000000000000001, while 0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3) gives 0.6. A computer stores decimals with a limited number of bits, and every addition drops a little of the trailing digits, so adding in a different order can give a result that differs in the last digit. This is not a Python flaw; any program that computes with floating-point numbers behaves this way.

deep-dive-zero.paragraphs.1.text: For every token the model writes, it does hundreds of millions of multiplications and additions. To be fast, the server splits this work across many compute units, runs them at the same time, then combines the results, and how it splits the work can change with how many requests were batched together. You can't control which requests yours is batched with each time, so the scores computed for the same request twice can differ in the last few digits.

deep-dive-zero.paragraphs.2.text: Most of the time this small difference doesn't matter: the top candidate leads by so much that no change in the last digits affects the ranking. The trouble comes when two candidates are nearly tied. A made-up example: at some step "Meow" has a score of 2.00001 and "Cat" has 2.00000. An error that only needs to lower "Meow" by 0.00002 makes "Cat" the top one. Temperature 0 still takes the top one; the top one just changed. From this step on, everything continues from "Cat".

deep-dive-zero.paragraphs.3.text: There are two more sources that have nothing to do with computation. One is that providers update models, and the same model name can end up pointing to a different version. The other is that some providers offer a random seed parameter so that the draw can be replayed, but their documentation also promises only best-effort consistency. Temperature 0 greatly reduces the fluctuation, but it can't be treated as a guarantee that the same request always gets the same answer.

misconception-zero.claim.text: If I set temperature to 0, the same request will always get exactly the same answer, so in tests I can compare them character for character.

misconception-zero.correction.text: Temperature 0 only means taking the highest-probability candidate at each step. The answer is usually very stable, but the provider does not guarantee it is identical character for character: computation error, batched computation, and model updates can all change the result. In a test, either run it several times to see the fluctuation, or check conditions the program can verify, such as format and required content, instead of requiring identical text.

section-5.title.text: How the lab report counts "how many different answers"

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: The number of different answers is counted by the program: it strips leading and trailing whitespace and then compares character by character, so a difference of even one punctuation mark counts as two. Put the 5 answers together: are "Meow Mart" and "Meow Mart." the same? What about "Meow Mart" and "Meow Store"? If a person judges, different people may decide differently, and the conclusion can't be rechecked.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: count_distinct first uses strip to remove the whitespace and newlines at the start and end of each answer, then puts them into a set and counts the elements in the set. A set only cares whether strings are exactly the same: one extra period counts as another answer, and answers with similar meaning are not merged. The lab report also lists how many times the most frequent answer appeared, and a table with the original text of the 5 answers.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: This number only answers "how many different strings". If 3 of the 5 are different, they could be three completely different shop names, or just differ in punctuation, so read the number together with the table. The system prompt asks for only the shop name and no punctuation, also so that character-by-character comparison means something: if you had the model write a shop introduction, it would differ almost every time, and this number would show you nothing.

mq-zero-two-kinds.zero-two-kinds.prompt.text: With temperature set to 0, four of the 5 answers are "Meow Mart" and one is "Cat Corner Shop". Which explanation is plausible?

mq-zero-two-kinds.zero-two-kinds.a.text.text: At some step two candidates were nearly tied, and a tiny difference in computation made one of the runs take the other

mq-zero-two-kinds.zero-two-kinds.a.feedb.text: Correct. At temperature 0 each step takes the top candidate, but the top one can change because of computation error, and then everything after it differs.

mq-zero-two-kinds.zero-two-kinds.b.text.text: The 5th request carried the answers of the first 4

mq-zero-two-kinds.zero-two-kinds.b.feedb.text: Not quite. The request body is built only once, and the messages in all 5 are identical character for character. You can check the 5th request on the timeline.

mq-zero-two-kinds.zero-two-kinds.c.text.text: The provider must have ignored the temperature parameter

mq-zero-two-kinds.zero-two-kinds.c.feedb.text: You can't conclude that. Some providers do ignore temperature for certain models, but this kind of difference can also appear when temperature does take effect. This one observation can't tell the two apart.

mq-zero-two-kinds.zero-two-kinds.explana.text: Temperature 0 only means taking the highest-probability candidate at each step. It doesn't guarantee identical text every time.

section-6.paragraphs.0.text: One run is just one sample: it shows what happened this time, not that it will happen every time. Back to the opening question: in {{lesson:chat-request}} each of the two arms ran once and the answers differed, and you couldn't tell whether that was the system prompt's effect or the fluctuation sampling has anyway. Now you know that even without changing a single character of the request, the answer changes.

section-6.paragraphs.1.text: A controlled experiment changes one condition and keeps everything else the same. The two arms in this lesson do that: same model, same messages, only temperature changed. Even so, each arm has to be run several times: first see how large the fluctuation inside one arm is, then see whether the difference between the two arms is bigger than that fluctuation. Only when the difference shows up steadily can you say that condition caused it.

section-6.paragraphs.2.text: A made-up example: before changing the prompt you run 5 times and 3 meet the requirement; after the change you run 5 times and 4 do. It looks better, but running the same prompt another 5 times could just as well give 2 or 4, so a difference of 1 means nothing. If after the change several batches in a row get all 5 right and before the change it never went above 3, then the difference is worth believing.

section-6.paragraphs.3.text: Five runs are still very few. They are enough to show whether there is fluctuation and roughly how large it is, but not enough to give a number like "how often a given shop name appears at temperature 1.3". {{lesson:prompt-experiments}} reads its results the same way when comparing prompt rewrites. {{lesson:tool-proposals}} starts having the model propose calls: which tool to choose and what to fill in for the arguments are likewise drawn one token at a time.

mq-one-run.one-run-conclusion.prompt.text: You changed one character of the system prompt and ran once, and the answer got better. What can you conclude now?

mq-one-run.one-run-conclusion.a.text.text: Not yet: run several times before and after the change and see whether the difference is stable

mq-one-run.one-run-conclusion.a.feedback.text: Correct. Running the same request again could just as well get better or worse; the difference in one run may be just fluctuation.

mq-one-run.one-run-conclusion.b.text.text: The change works, because the answer really did get better

mq-one-run.one-run-conclusion.b.feedback.text: Not quite. A difference in one run may come from sampling, not necessarily from your change.

mq-one-run.one-run-conclusion.c.text.text: The change has no effect, because only one character changed

mq-one-run.one-run-conclusion.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The size of a change and its effect aren't necessarily related. Judge it by repeating the run.

mq-one-run.one-run-conclusion.explanatio.text: A single result is just one observation. To compare, fix the other conditions and run each arm several times.

code-decision.title.text: Count different answers by string, not by meaning

code-decision.by-meaning.title.text: Judge by meaning whether two answers count as the same

code-decision.by-meaning.why_not.text: That needs a person or another model to judge, and the judgment itself adds new uncertainty. This lesson counts only what the program can determine.

low-vs-high.title.text: Low and high temperature, 5 runs each

low-vs-high.hypothesis.text: The messages sent in both arms are exactly the same, and only temperature changes. At temperature 0, the 5 answers should have few different phrasings; at temperature 1.3 there should be more.

low-vs-high.temperature-sent.text.text: temperature in request 1: the only difference between the two arms.

low-vs-high.same-messages.text.text: messages in request 5: identical to request 1 character for character, and the earlier answers were not carried in.

low-vs-high.each-answer.text.text: The answer in each response: go through them one by one on the timeline and see whether it changes.

low-vs-high.answer-table.text.text: The lab report's table: the 5 answers listed side by side.

low-vs-high.distinct-count.text.text: The lab report's metrics: the number of different answers counted by the program, and the total usage of the 5 requests.

low-vs-high.guide.0.text.text: This run sent the same request 5 times. First confirm the experimental condition.

low-vs-high.guide.1.text.text: This is the only place the two arms differ.

low-vs-high.guide.2.text.text: The messages sent in request 5 are exactly the same as in request 1, and the earlier answers haven't been mixed in.

low-vs-high.guide.3.text.text: This is the answer from one of the runs. Step through a few more and see whether they are the same.

low-vs-high.guide.4.text.text: The table puts the 5 answers side by side so you can compare them one by one.

low-vs-high.guide.5.text.text: The number of different answers is compared character by character by the program. Run the other arm and compare this number.

low-vs-high.conclusion.proves.0.text: The 5 requests in this run had exactly the same content, so the differences between the answers come from the provider's side (the request did not change): above temperature 0 it is mainly sampling; at temperature 0 it may also be tiny computation errors, or the provider batching several requests together.

low-vs-high.conclusion.proves.1.text: How many different answers each temperature gave in these 5 runs.

low-vs-high.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: 5 runs are too few to give a stable proportion of answers at a given temperature; run another batch and the number of different answers may be different.

low-vs-high.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: That all 5 are the same at temperature 0 doesn't guarantee the 6th is too; some providers ignore this parameter for reasoning models.

low-vs-high.conclusion.does_not_prove.2.text: More varied answers aren't better or worse. This lesson does not judge answer quality.

quiz.temperature-shape.prompt.text: A made-up example: at some step the probabilities for "Meow", "Cat", "Cute", and "Pet" are 44%, 32%, 16%, and 8%. What happens when you lower the temperature from 1 to 0.5?

quiz.temperature-shape.a.text.text: "Meow" gets a bigger share, the lower-ranked candidates get smaller, and the order stays the same

quiz.temperature-shape.a.feedback.text: Correct. A low temperature sharpens the distribution and magnifies the gaps, but doesn't change the ranking.

quiz.temperature-shape.b.text.text: The ranking may flip, with "Cat" becoming first

quiz.temperature-shape.b.feedback.text: Not quite. Temperature changes only the gaps, not the order.

quiz.temperature-shape.c.text.text: The four probabilities stay the same, and temperature affects only the answer's length

quiz.temperature-shape.c.feedback.text: Not quite. Temperature changes exactly the share with which each candidate is drawn at every step.

quiz.zero-five-same.prompt.text: With temperature 0, the 5 answers are exactly the same. What can you conclude?

quiz.zero-five-same.a.text.text: These 5 were the same; it is not guaranteed that every future run will be

quiz.zero-five-same.b.text.text: At temperature 0 the model's output is fully deterministic

quiz.zero-five-same.c.text.text: The model cached the first answer and returned it directly afterward

quiz.zero-five-same.c.feedback.text: Not quite. Every request is generated afresh. The answers are the same because each step took the highest-probability candidate.

quiz.distinct-rule.prompt.text: Two answers are "Meow Mart" and "Meow Mart.". How many kinds does the program count when it counts different answers?

quiz.distinct-rule.a.text.text: 1 kind, since the meaning is the same

quiz.distinct-rule.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The count of different answers counts how many kinds of answer there are. Two that differ make 2 kinds.

quiz.distinct-rule.explanation.text: This number only shows whether strings are the same. Whether the meanings are similar is for you to judge from the table.

quiz.longer-more-variance.prompt.text: At the same temperature, why are two runs more likely to differ the longer the answer is?

quiz.longer-more-variance.a.text.text: Every token needs a draw; the more draws there are, the easier it is to go astray, and once one step diverges everything after it changes

quiz.longer-more-variance.a.feedback.text: Correct. Each step continues from what was written before, so if an earlier step differs, the whole rest differs.

quiz.longer-more-variance.b.text.text: When the answer gets long, the provider switches the request to another model

quiz.longer-more-variance.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The model is determined by the setting in the request and doesn't change with answer length.

quiz.longer-more-variance.c.text.text: The model deliberately changes its wording when writing long answers

quiz.longer-more-variance.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The difference comes from drawing by probability at each step, not from the model doing it on purpose.

quiz.longer-more-variance.explanation.text: The answer is drawn step by step; the more steps, the more chances to diverge.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Run either arm, find the last request sent, and confirm its messages are the same as in request 1.

check-hunt.explanation.text: The messages in request 5 are identical to request 1 message by message: the answers from the first 4 did not enter this request. The differences between the answers are not because the request changed.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare your own run with this lesson's source code, and tick each item once you have done it.

check-points.item-1.text.text: I compared request 1 of the two arms and confirmed they differ only in temperature.

check-points.item-2.text.text: I read the lab reports of both arms, compared the numbers of different answers, and also looked at the answers in the table one by one.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I changed temperature to 0.7 and ran again, and saw where the number of different answers falls between the two arms.

check-points.item-4.text.text: I can say what "all 5 the same at temperature 0" can prove and what it can't.

code_notes.count_distinct.note.text: Counts the different answers: strips leading and trailing whitespace, then compares character by character.
